utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I, at the outset, welcome you back for the continuation and the conclusion of this case, but I'm hearing not English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am to say that in the absence of Judge Mindua, we sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. I take this opportunity to give the Trial Chamber's decision on the application by the Defence for the admission of an expert report from Ivan Stamenov. The Defence intends to call Stamenov as the ballistics expert. We have a biography which details his educational background and his professional career. The Prosecution challenges the expertise of Ivan Stamenov in respect of sections 6 and 7 of the report which provide analysis and conclusions relating to sniping incidents. In particular, it submits that Stamenov, not being a police officer, does not possess sufficient expertise to comment on the accuracy of a police homicide investigation. According to the Prosecution, his expertise lies in the field of weapons evaluation, apparently without having had, according to the Prosecution, any training or expertise in sniping per se. To the extent that his expertise in competitive sports shooting and weaponry allow him to comment as an expert on sniping, he may do so, in the submission of the Prosecution, but the Prosecution questions the weight to be attached to such evidence. The Defence, in its first response, submits that it is not necessary to be a police officer to be able to comment on possible origin and direction of fire caused by infantry weapons. It further submits that Stamenov's analysis of the sniping incidents was based on a review of material that was disclosed by the Prosecution and the investigative documentation of the Bosnian Muslim police ballistic experts in light of other technical information required to determine the trajectory of a bullet. With regard to the Prosecution argument that Stamenov does not possess sufficient expertise to comment on police homicide investigations, the Defence submits that the only determination made by Stamenov is that the material provided to him did not contain the information necessary to pronounce on the direction of fire or the nature of the projectile that injured the alleged victim. The Chamber has reviewed the report of Stamenov and his biography. The biographical information shows that he has had a long military career during which he occupied several positions relating to the operation of weaponry and target practice. In addition, his experience in competitive shooting indicates that he is, at the very least, familiar with shooting targets from various ranges. As such, he can be considered an expert in ballistics. The Trial Chamber finds that he is qualified to testify as an expert and that the objections raised by the Prosecution relate to matters that should be tested in cross-examination so that the Trial Chamber may assess the weight to be attached to the evidence. That's the Trial Chamber's decision on Ivan Stamenov's report. I turn next to the report of Prsic, and here I would just like to ask questions of the Prosecutor and the Defence. The Prosecutor makes the point, Mr. Tapuskovic, that two-thirds of this report was not written by the witness but was copied from another document, that document being a submission by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the International Court of Justice. I note that the expert, Mr. Prsic, did not acknowledge this source, and I am to ask Mr. Tapuskovic whether this is not a shocking case, that why should the Chamber accept a report from a person as an expert when two-thirds of it is not his work and he has not even acknowledged the source? Is this not substantially plagiarism? Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I must say that the material on the basis of which Professor Prsic worked is primarily the documentation that the Defence had requested from the then-existing Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and pursuant to the decision that was made at the time by the president of the state that existed then, which was the union of Serbia and Montenegro, Mr. Svetozar Marovic, we received a lot of documentation, among which the first document was not the one cited by the Prosecution as the response of that state which was another state in 1995. Nobody's able to understand this anymore. So it's not that one that was used. I made available to the Prosecution that decision of the federal government, the then-federal government, signed by the president, Mr. Svetozar Marovic, and the first document quoted there is called, "Relevant Events in Bosnia-Herzegovina Related to the War." It's a 76-page document, a working document. And of course I drew the attention of the expert to that documentation. It is very voluminous documentation. And he made use of it. At this moment nobody can reinvent those historic facts in a new creative way. These documents provide certain information and I don't really think that that information concerning events preceding the twentieth century have great importance. I do not know how the Trial Chamber is going to assess events from that historical perspective. Mr. Prsic gave that background information. Historical facts cannot be changed and he quoted the sources. He used the documentation I gave him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But without acknowledging that it came from another source. He presented it as his own so that we would have been left to form the conclusion that the analysis was his own and the conclusions were his own, when in fact they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course you will take that into account, Your Honours, but I believe that in that field of expertise, historical documents and historical facts cannot be interpreted. It is true that parties to the conflict both tell their different histories, but I don't think that segment of the report is really that important. What matters to the Defence is what happened 10 or 15 years before the conflict, the constitutional changes and the rest. Of course, it is up to you to attach a certain weight, if any, to those historical aspects. But as to the events that immediately preceded the conflict, I believe the findings of the expert can be useful to you. Of course, I leave this evaluation to you, and if you believe that this is something that resembles or constitutes plagiarism, it is your decision. That expert can -- what he can do is he can say, I received these documents from the federal government, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Docherty, the Defence, through Mr. Tapuskovic, makes the argument that it doesn't matter that two-thirds of the report is taken from another document because it represents something that is historical, that's a fact. He says you can't reinvent the wheel here. What's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, I have two responses, Mr. President. First of all, the Defence does say that it doesn't matter, but they do so in a curious way. They say the events written about in that two-thirds of the report are unimportant, curiously taking the position that two-thirds of the report is excess or redundant or not necessary, which begs the question of why it was presented to the Chamber in the first place if it doesn't matter. But over and above that, accepting the Defence's, I guess, rather philosophical position that the past is what it is and is not capable of fresh interpretation, the fact is that what was put before this Chamber was not a recitation of historical fact, you know, on such and such a date so and so was elected, sort of thing, but an analysis of those facts. And what one expects an expert historian to bring to a Trial Chamber such as this is not a merely chronological recitation of events but an analysis of those events and an explanation of why those events matter to the issues that are before this Trial Chamber for determination. And that was presented by Dr. Prsic as his own analysis when, in fact, it was not his own analysis. And I will confess that we on this side of the courtroom were somewhat surprised when we asked the Defence about the correspondence, down to paragraph numbers, between the report that was submitted and the submission that was made to the International Court of Justice. We were expecting to hear that Dr. Prsic had had some role in drafting the document that went to the International Court of Justice and that therefore, although unacknowledged, this had in fact been, at least in part, his own work. But Dr. Prsic instead denied any knowledge of the submission to the International Court of Justice, which is not a tenable position given the correspondence between the two documents. So I guess I would agree with the Defence that while historical facts are what they are, almost anyone can look those facts up in an archive. What we're looking for from an expert is analysis and interpretation, and in this case we did not get Dr. Prsic's analysis and interpretation. We got the analysis and interpretation of whoever it was - and we don't know who it was - that authored the document that he copied. In making a submission such as this, of course, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence lay down criteria for circumstances under which a Defence expert -- an expert report from either party may be accepted or rejected. And expert reports should not be accepted from witnesses who do not have the necessary expertise. When one looks at Dr. Prsic's curriculum vitae, he has the appropriate degrees and has studied the appropriate subjects. But even people who are experts in a field have areas they know very well and areas that they do not know all that well within their field. And the Prosecution's submission is that if Dr. Prsic found it necessary to turn in the work of another, our assumption is that he did so because he was not able to do his own original analysis, and that if in fact he was unable to do his own original analysis, that is circumstantial evidence, his academic degree notwithstanding, that he is not qualified to opine as an expert on the subjects that are discussed in this report. And it is for that reason that the Prosecution submits that the Defence expert's historical report should not be accepted into evidence on the grounds that the author of that report lacks the necessary expertise to give an opinion to this Chamber on those matters. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll give a decision on this matter later. Let the witness be called in. Your next witness, Mr. Tapuskovic, that's the Witness Demurenko, and his cross-examination, you will remember, is to be continued on the basis of the further documentation provided. The Prosecutor will have another 50 minutes to cross-examine Mr. Demurenko and then we'll have the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, you remain subject to the declaration that you gave earlier in these proceedings. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm very happy to be here before this Court again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have a few subjects for you in the remaining time allocated in cross-examination. I will also refer to a few of the photos you have provided the Trial Chamber with. But let me first start with going back to the statement you gave to the Bosnian Serb TV. Do you remember that? I think there is an issue, Mr. President, with translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. There is no translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's all right. I love the languages of Yugoslavia but not to that degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was trying to determine, Mr. Waespi, whether the cross-examination, the further cross-examination, is not to be confined to the matters that would arise from the additional documentation or whether you're still at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I hope so, Mr. President. I think I only used about two-thirds of my time so I have an additional, I think, 50 minutes and I'm quite confident I will conclude within this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you understand us now, Colonel Demurenko?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, going back to that TV interview you gave, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And at no time did you disagree in your interview with the technical findings of the Bosnians or other investigators, e.g., for instance, in relation to their findings as to likely descent or the bearing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not dispute that. Moreover, it formed the basis of my own inquiry. I wanted to show in principle that we took as a basis those primary findings made by the specialists in artillery and ballistic experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So the only issue is really whether the locations you visited were suitable, you know, to fire a 120-millimetre mortar from or whether it was possible because, as you put it, of the trees or the thickness of forests or the steepness of the terrain. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in principle. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If photo 03498 could be retrieved, and this, Mr. President and Colonel Demurenko, is a still from that video interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it shows that you looked at a JNA firing table for an M52, 120-millimetre mortar, M52. Is that correct? I'm sure it will be retrieved in a second. I can ask you while that's being done: Do you recall that you based your calculations of the distances on a JNA 120-millimetre mortar, model M52?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right. It was based on the initial information presented by the ballistic experts. I had sent those materials before. I'm not showing you anything new. The only document, and that's the reason why I brought this material with me, is that this is the first copy of the initial inquiry with my handwritten notes on it. I sent you that material before but I'm now bringing it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. With that I think we might come to those documents perhaps later. But there is no evidence on the record that an M52 was used by -- allegedly used by the Bosnian Serb army. The evidence is - perhaps you're aware of that - that an M74 was used by the Bosnian -- by the Bosnian Serb army, as evidenced, for instance, for everybody's benefit, in Prosecution Exhibit 252 on page 2.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to one thing. The 120-millimetre mortar produced by the Soviet Union was in the arsenal of the entire former Yugoslavia. After the breakup of Yugoslavia, those 120-millimetre mortars remained in all the parts of the former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Croatia, in Serbia, everywhere. So it's one and the same system regardless of the particular model, M52 or M54. It's one and the same gun with the same firing tables. It did not change. It was not modified by the Yugoslav People's Army. The Yugoslav People's Army had no capacity for such modification. That is the firing table that applies to 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But I suggest to you, Colonel, that the M74 that was, according to the evidence - and there is no other evidence on the record - used by the Bosnian Serb army has a different firing table with different data leading to different distances, according to the six charges, than an M52.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that evidence you are referring to. I inspected, in the course of my duty, all the units of the warring parties and I saw with my own eyes that the 120-millimetre mortar was used by the warring parties, the kind that I am using as an example, without any restriction. I saw that same mortar on both sides. I really don't know what evidence you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So let's assume that, for the sake of the argument, that your calculations or the basis you had in order to find out where to go was right, and let's talk about the bearing, the degree from which the alleged mortar was fired from. You looked at a direction of 176 degrees out of a full circle of 360 degrees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you understand, I am not -- I can't remember the figures now, but I have in my hands the document and it contains different figures to the ones that you are quoting. And that was the primary basis for my inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But let me just go back to what you told us last time and it comes from your TV interview, and that's on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second, please, Mr. Waespi. You just said that you have a document in your hand which shows different figures from the ones quoted by the Prosecutor. What is that document? And tell us, what are the different figures in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just heard the number 176 degrees. The table that I have before me contains different numbers. There is no such number there, 176 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps it could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like it to be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps he can put it on the ELMO, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's a document the witness -- no, this part, I think, Mr. President, is already in evidence, but it only shows the angle of descent which is something I am not discussing at this point in time. I'm interested in the direction of fire, you know, where it came from. If you have a circle of 360 degrees, there is evidence, and I think the Colonel said last time, that he drew a line of 176 degrees and he says that on page 7.700. And on that line of 176 degrees, he visited three or four locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Waespi, I just want the record, the transcript, to show, to be clear, as to which document the witness is referring. This is from his set of papers that he has submitted. You say this is already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If you give me a moment, I can try to find the exact place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while it is on the screen, while this drawing is on the screen, could the witness tell us what it is while it's still on the screen? He has been shown that picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he should tell us what it is, and for the record I want it to be clearly identified. If it's already in evidence, what is the exhibit number, and this is perhaps more for the benefit of my staff which will have to be preparing summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's 254, Mr. President, Prosecution Exhibit 254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 254. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it has markings by the witness. It's obviously the report by the Bosnian experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a document prepared by the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And it was tendered in February by Prosecution witness, protected witness 137. I'm grateful to Mr. Sachdeva for that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this exhibit talks about the angle which the shell was hitting the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an image that I made. The angle of descent is shown in this document. It's a document presented and drafted by an expert from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What matters principally is this: I did not dispute the findings of BH experts. I set out to be impartial and I said, Sector Sarajevo agrees with your initial findings regarding a possible mortar attack and the angles shown here. But from there on I spoke about the fact that even if this is true, even if all this is accurate, this angle of descent, then further investigation would show that this shell could not have come from Serbian territory, or rather, territory controlled by Bosnian Serbs. That was all. I did not want to go into the technical details, the costliness of that angle and all the other findings. I said this initial drawing is correct, but now I'm going to expose your attempt to blame it on Bosnian Serbs as an aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the bearing now, the direction of fire the alleged shell was fired from. And you mentioned the figure of 200 -- 2.850, more or less, mils, and that equals about 160 degrees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while you think about your answer, if Exhibit P357 could be retrieved, please, on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What I'm really interested in now, and if you can focus on the direction of fire, where the shell allegedly was fired from. The Prosecution says from the Bosnian Serbs. So please focus on a circle of 360 degree, and I understand your evidence from last time that you said you were looking at an angle, a bearing, direction of fire, of 176 degrees which is, in a 360 circle, slightly less than half, slightly less than 180 degrees. Do you remember having said last time that you went to look at locations that were located at a line of 176 degrees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you have asked several questions. Perhaps they are aspects of the same question, but first you asked the witness to say whether he agreed that 2.850 mils was more or less equal to 160 degrees, or was equal to 160 degrees. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not prepared now to defend certain details or trig points, degrees, and azimuths for a certain reason: Too much time has elapsed to claim with certainty now whether it was 167, 175, or 160. What I'm talking about is the principle. In the material that I sent to this honourable court there is some material that I had given in the TV interview and this is -- what I'm holding now is the first copy written in my own hand as a result of my inquiry. Now, I'm not prepared to talk about numbers and fractions, but I can answer the second question: Yes, I personally visited all those locations that were determined as possible origins of fire, and that is, I believe, part of the material before your court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness, I think, brought with him a piece of paper which might have been drawn by him, and I think if that could be put onto the ELMO. This is, I think, DD00-4398. Yes, that's the piece of paper the witness brought with him. If that could be put onto the ELMO. I thought the witness had a different sketch that was part of the -- yes, that's the one I'm interested in, if it could be turned around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, here, Witness, you see that you talk in the second line, the handwritten part, about direction of fire, 2.850 mil, and I suggest to you that this figure comes from the French report and that figure of 2.850 mils equals about 160 degrees in a full circle of 360 degrees. Would you agree with that or is that too much figures? We can move on if you don't want to answer these figures, as you pointed out a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I just want to confirm that this drawing that is placed in evidence and the one before me, they're practically the same, although mine is a bit different. That was indeed part of my inquiry and I have my conclusions and point of view that hasn't changed since then. I insist that that was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But the more specific question is whether you agree that 2.850 mils equals about 160 degrees in a full circle of 360. You had earlier answered that question by saying, if my recollection is correct, that you would not wish to be specific, you wouldn't wish to commit yourself. Do you maintain that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true for a simple reason. It is not at all difficult to locate an inaccuracy if we start playing with one-thousandths, decimal point, and so on. It is impossible for me to remember all of the figures that used to be in my head during the war and later. So if you're trying to catch me in a discrepancy that I mentioned a figure of 160 and then 170, then it won't be difficult at all. I would rather not go into the discussion of the angle of descent and the decimal points. What I would rather focus on is whether the interpretation of the figures was done accurately. And this discussion of decimal points won't lead us to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I accept that, Colonel Demurenko, Mr. President. What I'm trying to do is just figure out what the line of direction was that gave you the guidance to go out into the field and look at these specific locations. And the way I understand your evidence of last time is that you drew a line of 170 degrees and you went out and looked at three or four locations. 176, yes, 176 degrees. And that's what you said on Bosnian TV and that's what's recorded in the transcript of last time. I don't want to play with figures. I don't want to kind of try to trick you. Not at all. I just want to figure out, where did you go into the field in the aftermath of 28th of August, 1995? So 176 degrees, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm prepared to assure you that I stand by everything I said, both in my interview and in my previous court testimony. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look now at the map of that area south of Markale, and it's 03399. Colonel, the basis for drawing up this map was your testimony that you went -- you drew a line of 170 degrees and you went out and looked at the locations of possible mortar sites at distances 2.000, 2.700, 3.400, and 3.600. And if you look at this map, you can see the left line represents 176 degrees. It's almost half circle, 180 degrees. And the line to the left would be 170 degrees, and 160 degrees would be even more to the right. That's what the French were -- so you visited, if I understand you correctly, for instance, location on the left line, 176 degrees, at 3.400 and 3.600 metres. You can see those two locations, distances, left of reference point C. That's what our conclusion is. Is that a fair conclusion by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a contradiction here. The map that you're showing to me right now has different figures that differ from the ones on the sheet in front of me. If I need to compare them, at least I didn't draw in the blue lines onto the map. Somebody else, another group, did this. I had just one line that was based on the angle of descent as shown by the expert of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that I verified. Now, these figures that I've been shown, 160 and 170 and then 176, that is making the analysis so much more complex that we can spend quite a lot of time on it now. I'm not prepared to confirm what I see in front of me. These figures need to be verified. I didn't draw this. Who did this? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the Prosecution would need to verify when this drawing was made, whether it was made at the time of the incident or later, and by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness said last time when he came - and I'm quoting reference on page 7.700, at line 11 - "that according to the results of the investigation, the line of fire was 176 degrees." So that's the basis for the left line. Then next the witness said on page 7.701, on lines 17 to about 22: "The following three possibilities for firing were at 3.700 metres, 3.400 metres and 3.600 metres." We took the last two distances the witness pointed out last time and put it onto the line of direction of fire, 176 millimetres. And the witness then continued and said: "I visited the location today with my own expert group. We were here and here and here. And I have no doubt in my mind that this place was unacceptable, that no shell could have come from here." An investigator of the OTP went to visit the same locations and we brought photos with us, and I would like the photos to show on those spots the witness claims to have visited - perhaps it was the wrong spots - and confront it to the witness. That's the purpose of this exercise, Mr. President. I don't put any words into the mouth of the witness. We just analysed what he said last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that the two lines, Mr. Waespi, on the map, 176 degrees and 170 degrees, are lines drawn by the Prosecution and which you say reflect accurately what the witness said in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Only the left line relates to what the witness said, because he said 176 degrees. 170 degrees is based on evidence other witnesses pointed out in court, for instance, Mr. Konings. But I haven't come to that part yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to make a comment. I want to object to the fact that this was done now, after the testimony of Witness Demurenko. The basic rule of the adversarial system was not applied here; namely, that the parties needed to go together to the spot at the same time, in which case we would have been able to know for a fact that this was done the way it was explained by Mr. Waespi. We should have been given an opportunity to follow this analysis. The rights of the parties have been violated here. The equality of arms principle was violated because we should have been present when the Prosecution went to visit the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you have made several statements in these proceedings about the adversarial system and some of them are just not accurate. The essence of the adversarial system is that it is a party system. One party makes an allegation and the other party has a right to comment on it or to contradict it. There is absolutely nothing wrong with what the Prosecutor did. You have commented on it. You have challenged it. And so that in assessing the weight to be attached to this aspect of the evidence, the Trial Chamber will take into account the point that you have made. Now, let us proceed, Mr. Waespi, and let us try to move quickly and move away from this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll do my best, but it's a very important point, Mr. President. If this map -- we might come back to it, but if it could get an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P921, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have already made a ruling and I don't want to question that ruling. I just wanted to be on the record that I, as Defence counsel, objected to this being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. Well, my colleague is asking why, but I expect it is for the reasons you have already stated. Do you want to hear them again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps I can also put on the record that on the 26th of July, we disclosed all the photos, and the fact that the investigator Barry Hogan went to investigate these sites. Mr. President, if the other exhibit the witness referred to, the chart with, you know, the handwritten parts above the line, could also be exhibited for the transparency of the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P922, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If photo 03482 could be displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, the investigator went to that site at 3.600 metres on the line of 176 degrees. You say you have visited, in the aftermath of Markale, and dare we say that you have no doubt in mind that this place was unacceptable, that no shell could have come from here. And I would like you to have a look at this place and tell us whether you recognise that location. Do you remember having visited that location when you went out to look at possible sites of firing of a 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that the appearance of the hills and slopes and the grass is something that I recognise, but I wish to tell you that at the time of the war - and this is where the front line was - this was not a site that one could come across. Everything looked completely different. All the houses were damaged. There were no cars and so on. If you go to visit this location 12 years later, you will see that it looks completely, completely different than what it did at the time of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, taking into account the passing of 12 years' time, that it's very likely, it's almost certain, that this location more or less looked the same 12 years ago and that you could fire 120-millimetre mortar anywhere from this area. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because, as I already explained on the last occasion I was here, a mortar cannot hang in the air. It is a very heavy piece of equipment, a mortar. It needs to lean heavily on a base and the base leaves a trace in the ground that cannot be concealed. So whenever one fires from a mortar, there are always traces left, traces of firing, traces of gunpowder, of the impression left in the ground, and also the traces of the transport that was used to bring in a mortar. One needs either a horse at a minimum or a vehicle to transport a mortar. So this is something that can be seen on the ground and recorded by a photograph; namely, if one compares the firing tables with all the figures, one can only come to the conclusion that a mortar could not have been placed there. And now to show photographs and to tell us that theoretically a mortar could have been placed there, then yes, this is perhaps a conclusion that one can draw in 2007. But 12 years ago it was absolutely an impossible conclusion to make because it was impossible to conceal the traces of a mortar being placed there, and there was no trace of any mortars being placed there when we visited the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now that's a different argument, traces of trucks, traces of embedding a mortar into the ground. What your argument was until right now was that it was impossible to fire because of the thickness of the woods, because of the steepness of the terrain. Both of these arguments don't apply here. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, but the conclusion that it was impossible to fire from there was based either on the fact that there was a forest there and one could not place a mortar there and fire from it, or perhaps it was a rocky slope where one could not place a mortar, or it was a case of a clear meadow where there were absolutely no traces of a mortar being placed there. And I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that 12 years ago, in 1995, there was a rocky slope here and there was a forest here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the photograph that is in front of me now? No, I'm not claiming that. All I'm saying refers to the sites shown in the investigation. I am not sure at all that the photograph you're showing to me now was a site that I toured myself back 12 years ago. I'm not sure of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The only information we have, Colonel, is what you told us last time. A bearing of 176 degrees and the several locations, 3.400, 3.600, you claim to have visited. That's the basis of us sending the investigator and to find these pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But his answer to that is that he's not sure at all that the photograph on the screen was a site that he toured himself 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That would be my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How did you actually figure out where you were? Did you have a GPS at that time? How did you determine you actually reached, for instance, 3.400 metres' distance from Markale?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that the last time I was here. It is very easy to establish that. As I said before, a shell for 120-millimetre mortar has only six standard charges, and if one applies a minimum charge --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I understand how you came to determine that you want to go o see a location at 3.400 metres. But how did you actually figure out that you were now at a distance of 3.400 metres from Markale?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where the problem is. You just draw a line from a possible firing location, or, rather - interpreter's correction - from a possible site of explosion and then you draw a line to a possible firing location. We have in the military very precise instruments, such as GPS and some other instruments, which can calculate down to a millimetre the location, instruments such as laser devices, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And at that time you had a GPS?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have always had such a device for orientation, ever since the Americans put it in use. It's a universal military system. In addition to GPS, there are many other methods to calculate the chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, but which one did you use? What method did you actually use? Was it GPS? Was it laser? What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a complex approach, a multi-facetted approach. We tried to establish accurately down to a metre this location at 3.600 metres' elevation. It was a complex approach so as no -- that nobody could challenge the results of our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So did you visit this location, if you recall after so many years; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the sites mentioned in my investigation, I toured all of them, and you can see the photographs. Unfortunately, I wasn't able to find all of the photographs in my own archive. Now, to claim that I visited precisely this spot, I wouldn't be able to do that because I'm 100 per cent sure that there were no buildings -- these buildings were not there. And I can assure you that this was not the location shown in the photographs because the site that I visited had no houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a fairly large meadow, as we see from a satellite picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if, first of all, this image could have an exhibit number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, which of the locations is shown on the photo? Is it the 3.400 metres' distance or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is 3.600 metres, Judge Harhoff. We also have 3.400 metres and I could -- we have photos of all the locations, but I wanted to leave it at this one but show a satellite image which shows all the locations we have visited. But this particular one is, indeed, 3.600 metres, a large meadow, a house on it. If we -- if that could be tendered as an exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P923, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have one without houses? Because the witness says it's almost certain that the sites that he visited didn't have any houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We could try the distance 3.400 metres on the same line, 176 degrees. This is ter number 03484.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While that's being done, we might come to your pictures in a moment. But I recall that there was also a picture, a meadow, a house, and even a cow. Was that one of the locations you had visited which were possible firing positions of mortars?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that the photographs that I sent to you depict the sites that I personally toured and where I personally could confirm that no mortars could have been placed there, and the photographs serve as evidence of that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just before turning to this photo, what you just talked about is your photo, that meadow, a house, and a cow on it. I see no thickness of forest there --

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let's leave the discussion about your photograph for a moment. Let's turn to this one, this photograph. As I pointed out, this is on the 176-degree line. This is 3.400 metres and that's one of the locations you claim to have visited. Do you recall having visited this location? And just one part of it, of this fairly large meadow, do you recall having been at this location?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have a hard time hearing Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters are having a hard time hearing you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's a technical issue. Perhaps the technicians could come in or Mr. Tapuskovic could come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's been suggested that you come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're using something else today and I'm quite confused now. It's a bit complicated. It's a clip-on mic and it seems to have slipped. Your Honours, I don't think we will get anywhere by showing such small parts of a large photograph. If the Prosecution has a larger view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is well able to protect himself. Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm prepared, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, the question as it was phrased is not a proper one. To ask me whether I visited such a site is basically an impossible task. I can neither confirm nor deny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's an improper comment for you to make. It's the Chamber that will determine whether the question is proper or not. Just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, would you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. My question was: Do you recall having visited this possible launching of a mortar site after 28th July 1995? And for your information, this is on the 176-degree line at 3.400 metres, so about 200 metres away from the picture we saw beforehand.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't understand why 200 metres. The range of a mortar is not 200 metres. As I said, the maximum range is 5.400 metres. The minimum one is 1.000. So the appropriate distance is 600 to 800 metres, I mean the steps between various firings are 600 to 800, not 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm going to stop you. Quite apart from the technical points you are making, do you have any recollection of visiting this particular site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I cannot say for sure that I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I expected you to say. Mr. Waespi, I'm not sure where this is taking you, whether it's a valuable technique.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To show the witness a particular site, there is nothing special about it. We see grass and we see some shrubs. What is there about it that would make the witness recall it? It seems that you will always get the answer which the witness has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, this witness has said that he visited three, perhaps four, very precisely identified locations, and he said it was impossible to fire mortars. He didn't say, I did not find any traces. He said it was impossible because of the rockiness of the terrain, the steepness of the terrain, because of the thickness of the forest. We did send an investigator and it's properly fine to launch a 120-millimetre mortar from the very locations the witness said he has visited, and that's the purpose of this exercise, to show the witness these locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand, but the witness is not agreeing that the sites which are depicted on the screen are sites that he visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And the proper conclusion, then, from the Prosecution is the witness at that time did not visit these locations he claimed to have visited for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't give us that now. You can give us that in your closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you asked me where is it leading us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- it's a matter for you to submit on in your closing -- in your closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, perhaps you would also explain to us how your investigator located this particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff, he had a GPS available and we have given to the Defence photos which shows the palm of the investigator with the GPS on it. If that photo could have an exhibit number, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P924, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And another issue I omitted to raise is to tender the still from that video which shows the M52 the witness referred to. If that could be exhibited as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P925, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the following satellite photo, 03480, could be retrieved, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel, you will see on the next photo again the same two lines, this time in the white. On the left side it's 176 degrees, the line you claim was your guidance to visit these locations. On the right side is 170 degrees, other witnesses have said was the likely direction of fire. Now, you see in black, WP2, 3, 4. These are all the locations our investigator has visited and we have photos from all these locations disclosed to the Defence. Now, do you accept, Witness, just looking at the satellite picture, granted 12 years after the event, it appears that there is a number of possible - I say possible - locations where mortars could be fired into the city of Sarajevo on the 28th August 1995? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to answer this question in greater detail. Of course in theory, looking at this photograph and seeing these clearings, at least on the last two points, theoretically a mortar could be placed. But I don't understand why you have mentioned already twice my own arguments. I never said that all possible firing points were on rocky slopes, in the middle of a forest, and such like. Moreover, I gave you some photographs and I don't understand why you are not showing them. They show that I was on absolutely flat surfaces, in clearings covered with pristine grass. A mortar could be placed there. But our expert who scrupulously looked and investigated saw no traces of an actual mortar there. If you show my photographs, there are the rocky slopes which I point at with my finger; there are meadows there. Yes, there were meadows, but they were flat and clear, like the floor in this room. It was obvious nobody had placed a mortar there. And you are making me out as saying or having said that all of the terrain was rocky slopes and forests. I didn't say that. Now, look at this photograph, and if we see this line, 170 degrees, you can say that yes, there are clearings there and meadows. But that doesn't prove anything. Maybe 20 years later, there are slopes there. Sorry, 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all, there are two sources, Colonel, for our allegation or for my point that the only argument you have advanced were that it was impossible to fire mortars from the location. It's new today to hear that you say it was possible to fire but you didn't see traces. That's an argument I have not heard. But let me just go back to what you said last time, and I have quoted once before today. You said, quote from page 7.701, lines 19 to 22: "I visited the location today with my own expert group. We were here and here and here, and I have no doubt in my mind that this place was unacceptable, that no shell could have come from here. There is no possibility to fire a shell from this position at the place where it actually landed." There is no mentioning of, it's possible but there are no traces. You said "No possibility."

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's taken out of context, that's what it's called, because at the time I was giving the interview, I already had in my possession the photographs that already showed me pointing my finger on flat surfaces, clear surfaces, not only rocky slopes. But the fact is you can interpret the word "impossible" in different ways. You can interpret it narrowly, like physically impossible, and you can interpret it broadly, meaning that it was impossible to fire from there and then destroy all the traces of placing a mortar. It's your interpretation of the word "no possibility" or "impossible" that's very narrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we are coming to the break and I believe to the -- should be to the end of your cross-examination, the 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'd love to have 10 more minutes, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If this photo could be saved as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 200 - I'm sorry, Your Honours - as P926.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I would like to conclude with two photos and perhaps a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel, if the first of these photos - and I only have a hard copy of your photos, Colonel - could be placed onto the ELMO. This is DD00-4406d. Now, can you explain us where this location is, or rather, was, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On every photograph I point with my own hand the point that would have been a firing point, according to the schematic. So on every photo it's 15 to 30 metres away from me. We determined the point. I go out there and the photographer takes a snapshot of me as I am pointing to the place that could have been potentially a firing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. We might go to a map in a moment. But just to conclude this photo, that looks like it's Sarajevo in the background; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is territory controlled by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, by the Bosnian Serb army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it looks like it's a perfect observation point, one of the many you, I'm sure, have visited when you toured around Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I had several dozen, thousands of such points. Let me remind you that we in the Sector Sarajevo covered dozens of square kilometres, dozens of hundreds of square kilometres. I didn't have time to tour all possible observation points.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just referring to this one. That looks like a great observation point over the city of Sarajevo. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean a nice vantage point that gives a great panorama to tourists, then yes. From the viewpoint of the militaryman, this point is of zero value. It gives the military nothing. It shows some houses, neighbourhoods. It gives you absolutely no idea of the adversary, let me put it that way, who is behind those hills. This one is not even that good, considering that's in a -- that it is in a forest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's only good for tourist purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But I suggest to you that it's perfect to see the hit of an artillery, of a motor shell, see the smoke, give corrections over the radio to a gunner. That would be a suitable point for that. Not for tourists, for any military person. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. If you look at the man who is closest to the camera and the clearing there, then it is a possible location. But let me draw your attention to one thing. The neighbourhood we're talking about, Markale, is not visible from this point. It is behind the hill and down the hill, at the foot of the hill. You couldn't see any smoke. We are now seeing the opposite side of Sarajevo, which is very, very distant from Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. In fact, I can't really see clearly. But I'm just putting to you that if one -- somebody wanted to fire into Sarajevo, into the visible parts, you could actually see the impact or at least the smoke. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What target? What installation are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just repeat. In theory, if somebody wanted to fire a shell from this place into the visible part of Sarajevo, the part of Sarajevo you could see on this picture, indeed, in reality, he could do that; he could observe the impact based on the smoke or other, you know, debris and give corrections. That would be possible.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, if we are to analyse all sorts of military activity, one can fire not only a mortar but a tank without even raising the gun barrel. You could fire directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If this could be an exhibit, Mr. President, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Colonel, which point is this photo taken on? Is that the 3.400 or the 3.600 metres' point on the 176-degree bearing, line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's certainly on that line. And second, I have to be honest, now I don't remember any longer which photograph pertains to which locations, because I sent a set of photographs and there were four photographs in total. I found three. My finger is pointing at the wooded area. It could be the 3.400. But to be perfectly honest, I don't remember which location it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you must be coming to the end now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give this an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is admitted as P927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For your last question, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel, all this you did as a Russian colonel rather than as UNPROFOR Chief of Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. My main position was as an employee of the UN, the military mission, chief of the Sector Sarajevo, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, part of the Russian contingent. And only after that I was practically unofficially the senior member of the Russian Battalion within the UNPROFOR. But I was first and foremost the Chief of Staff of the peacekeeping mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Waespi. Suppose he had done it as a Russian colonel rather than UNPROFOR Chief of Staff. What is the point that you are making?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's unusual UN personnel, and we have seen the blue helmets, blue caps, on the previous photo are supposed to act within the UNPROFOR mandate, not get instructions or act on behalf of their national contingent. And the witness said himself that I am a citizen of my country, and this is very, very different from an UNPROFOR general, UNPROFOR colonel, acting as an UNPROFOR, UN, neutral general. And my suggestion is that he acted, indeed, as a Russian, as he confirmed, because Russians had preferred treatment by the Bosnian Serb army and I wanted to ask the witness to comment about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that is being put to you very directly. Let us hear the answer -- your answer to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll be happy to. We are now really coming to the conclusion that I wanted to concentrate on. This is absolutely incorrect, to suppose that I refuted the results of the official inquiry as a Russian citizen. I acted, first of all, as a UN officer from the position of impartiality to any side, and that was my chief function. I did not engage in any direct confrontations or acquisitions. If I wanted to accuse the Bosniak army, I would have investigated only the first two locations and I would have determined that fire had come from there. But that was not my purpose. I was just trying to show that the accusations and determinations against Serbs were false. That doesn't mean that one side was worse than the other. My belief was that one needs to be fair to everyone. And I wanted to go against the monopoly of truth, the monopoly over truth that the porte-parole had at his press conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can I ask an additional question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But it's a fact that the Russian UNPROFOR members got preferred treatment by the Bosnian Serb army, by the accused, for instance, that they were not taken prisoners in May when all the other UNPROFOR or other UNPROFOR members were taken prisoners. The Russians were not. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm prepared to answer this. It's very simple. The soldiers of the Russian Battalion stationed in Gorazde were not captured for one simple reason. They were on the territory controlled by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, by Serbs. In order to capture or take hostage the Russian soldiers, one would need to break out of the front line, then capture the Russian soldiers and detain them. And that would have meant running the risk of huge losses. Sometimes we ran risks even on Serb territory, my soldiers and I. You always run risks. It doesn't really rather where the bullet is coming from, from which side, or whose shell is going to explode under our APC. We were running risks all the time, but we wanted only fairness and justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So the explanation is a tactical one. You can't push this any further, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tapuskovic, how long will you be in your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is very difficult for me to give an answer to that. It depends on how much time the Chamber allots me. The Chamber has insisted so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Since you are want to refer to the adversarial system, I should tell you that, well, certainly the one that I come from, re-examinations are usually short and to the point. It's not an opportunity for you to rehash matters. And I will give you about 40 minutes for re-examination, no more, if you need 40 minutes. Confine yourself to matters that arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will truly limit myself to just those issues. However, I would like an additional instruction from you as Defence counsel. This witness was asked to send in certain pieces of evidence that he mentioned and the witness did so. Now I would like to know whether I will be able to explore those pieces of evidence, the ones that the witness brought in or sent in, since they were mentioned here. In addition, I would like to explore with him other pieces of evidence. You said that all of them had to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As long as it arises out of cross-examination. It must arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is the criterion that is applicable and which you well know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I will definitely stick to what I have to stick to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness be shown P254, which was shown just a moment ago to the witness. This is a drawing dated the 29th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Demurenko, on the day when you gave the statement to the television, to the Associated Press journalist, if I remember well, you said that you had this drawing in mind and that this is what made you doubt the analysis of the person who performed this investigation and that this is what you said to the journalist of Associated Press. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely the drawing that was the basis for investigation. However, what made be doubt was not the drawing itself, no. I took the drawing as a firm fact. There were other things that made me question this. The first one was that two hours after the explosion, somebody was brave enough or stupid enough to accuse Serbs of that, and the second aspect that made me question this was that the very large number of victims in the street was due to just one shell, which in reality practically doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you saw this drawing, and based on your knowledge and your experience, can you tell us, did the mortar come in from the north or south, based on this drawing and based on the calculations on the drawing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the drawing one cannot say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that arises from cross-examination. I didn't go into north or south or terrorist attack or whatever. The witness insisted to use this photo, but I said I'm not interested in the angle of the descent but the direction of fire. That's at issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is obvious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, don't answer. Mr. Tapuskovic, let me hear what your -- what would your next question be following from this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next question concerning this is as follows: This is the Prosecution Exhibit 254. My next and only question is whether the witness saw Exhibit 253, the Prosecution exhibit. I'm not asking for any explanation in relation to 254, but I would like to know whether the witness saw another document also dated the 29th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi's objection to your question was that it didn't arise from cross-examination because he didn't concern himself with the angle of the descent but with the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but he explained here a number of things relating to his doubts about what he had learned on that day from various sources. That was the main motive and practically this is what Mr. Waespi's examination centred on for practically the whole day. This witness spoke about his doubts and what motivated him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe that is fair, Mr. Waespi. What is your answer to the question, the question that was put by Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours, could this other drawing also be shown to the witness. This is Exhibit 253, the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it can be, but let us have the witness' answer to the question that was objected to and which I'm allowing. Can you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: In addition to the drawing dated the 29th of August, 1995, did the witness receive from the same source another drawing also of the same date, and I would like this to be shown to the witness so that he can reply with a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. You asked the question originally and Mr. Waespi objected, and I have now ruled that the question may be answered. We now have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have it here. "Can you tell us, did the mortar come in from the north or south, based on this drawing and based on the calculations on the drawing?" What's your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the previous drawing, it is impossible to say from which direction the mortar came because there were buildings there. Looking at the drawings, one can see the buildings, how high they were, and it is clear that the direction, as drawn in, was from the south. But I didn't have this drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So these two drawings on the same date are showing two different directions; is that correct? One from the north and one from the south.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is a question, then my reply is yes. This is an additional proof of contradictions and unwillingness of officials and UNPROFOR to investigate the true cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't understand the basis for the Defence's question that these drawings are contradictory. Where does it say it came from the south or from the north? The building is the indication that -- and the building stands on the southern side of the road in both images. That suggests that it came from the south. Maybe I don't understand the point the Defence is making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you are now referring to the image that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Initially, or rather, yes, I am now referring to this drawing. As to the previous drawing, it shows a completely different direction. Both drawings were made on the same day. This one here is showing the south as the direction and the first one is showing north. At any rate, there are two possible directions. The one that was initially shown to the witness is the one that made him doubt this, and the other drawing was shown later. This other drawing is also already in evidence and we will have an expert commenting on this. Both drawings were made on the same day and they show two completely different directions. I just asked the witness whether he had also seen this second drawing and he said no. And I don't need to insist on this any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, could it be that Prosecution Exhibit 254 is seen from the west towards the east, while Prosecution Exhibit 253 is seen from the other direction, from the east towards the west?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My view is of no importance. At any rate two drawings were made on the 29th of August, one showing one direction and the other showing the other direction. It is my position that the first one shows north as the direction of the mortar and the other one shows south. Both documents were produced on the same day by the same service, and we have been dealing with these drawings for quite a long time and they show two completely different directions. All I did was ask the witness whether he had also seen the other drawing and he said that he had never seen it. And in a way, this second drawing could be more accurate. Now, my opinion perhaps is of no importance on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I see that the point is made, but that's clearly something I did note -- I understand you ruled, but that's not something I did in my cross-examination. That would have been perfect for examination-in-chief, to go into these details about angle of descent. But I understand that the Defence has finished the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another point, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, last time you said that you also had a number of documents that you did not bring with you to The Hague because you believed that those documents were under special UN regime, that you had no right to bring them in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the documents that you sent to the Court, is there an important document among them? I would like to show this document to you. It is marked as DD00-4407. It was marked ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber will allow you to refer to the documents produced by the witness and which were not addressed by the Prosecutor, and the Chamber recalls how this whole question arose. It arose in the following circumstances: That the witness claimed that he had documents which could support the points that he was making, and the Chamber said it would defer his cross-examination so as to allow him to produce those documents. Well, obviously, those documents which substantiated his case would not be relied on by the Prosecutor and so the only way to allow that would be to allow you to utilise those documents. The Chamber is, of course, entirely free to determine how the case is to proceed, and even though you are now re-examining, the Chamber will allow you to refer to those documents which substantiate the points he was making with, of course, the Prosecutor being given the right to further cross-examine on that. So that this is a re-examination which is rather unique. It's a re-examination coupled with an examination by you on those points which were not addressed by the Prosecutor but which you feel will substantiate the witness' line of argument. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The next document is, I understand, an UNPROFOR document which is confidential. It is confidential -- at least what appears from the face of it. It came from the witness' hands and it contains some, I think, sensitive information which may be old, 12 years ago, but it has code names at the end of the document. So just out of an abundance of caution, I would go into private session in order to discuss this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown DD00-4398.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, who made this drawing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this drawing correspond to what you have drawn for us here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, what does this represent, although I understand it was a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple. I tried to make a very simplified version of all the complex artillery and other calculations so that it is understandable to laypeople, people who have nothing to do with the war or the artillery. In the top part of the drawing we see a representation of a narrow street and the distance between two buildings and the place of explosion. Then in the broken line, the dotted line, we see the possible trajectories of the mortar shell that could have arrived from that direction. We see the line of separation between two armies, the front line between the Bosnian Muslims and the army of Republika Srpska. And we see the six positions that correspond to six possible mortar charges. They are in keeping in firing tables, and according to these firing tables, they show from where this shell could have come from, depending on what charge was used. This is understandable, I believe, to a child. We see also the possible deviation of the shell on the left, and on the right-hand side we see the slopes of mountains determined according to the map and we see possible firing positions either on the opposite side of the hill or on the side of the hill which is closer to Sarajevo. I made this so it is understandable to reporters, people who have nothing to do with the military. Apart from this drawing, nothing more is necessary. Practically everybody can understand this. We see those fire points that were on the Bosnian side. If we determine that fire could not have come from there, then it must have come from the other two firing points and then the other side would be responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.
