utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this into evidence as well, DD00-4398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the records indicate this was just admitted as P922.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now DD00-4403, could we see that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, who made this drawing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was made by a French serviceman who was a part of the first investigation team that was charged with the ballistic expertise, as far as I can remember. I see that the writing is in French and I think that this was done by a French expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does this depict? If you tell us -- if you know, please tell us, what does this left line mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the trajectory line or the building itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Since these are kind of new documents that the witness brings from home, I think it might be useful to first establish the foundation, you know, of the witness' knowledge, familiarity, with this document, why he talks about it. Otherwise, you know, it serves no purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he did say, in answer to the question, Who made this drawing, that as far as he could remember, it was made by a French serviceman who was part of the first investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but he's not called as an expert. I mean, what's the basis of him to now make a comment on a French report? Was that a report he has seen, he has waved to the cameras when he talked to Bosnian Serbs? I would just like to see a connection between this document and the gentleman's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a different point. If you want to object on that basis, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It is already an exhibit already, by the way. You'll remember one of the confidential witnesses talked about it and even made a drawing. I can mention the name of the witness in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But why can't he comment on it, Mr. Waespi? Why can't this witness comment on it? You say he doesn't have the expertise to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I thought these were documents which the witness brought with him from Russia, and I would like to see why is it in his file before he kind of mentions how -- to make some comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that's for you to raise in cross-examination. I see no valid objection to this witness commenting on this document. Yes. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask the witness, Mr. Demurenko, whether he had this document in his possession back when he was in Sarajevo. Did he perhaps analyse -- did he perhaps analyse this document back then along the lines that he has explained to us now?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember this document being part of the material that I analysed. I have a feeling that this document has an alternative source and it basically does not contradict the idea that I had during my investigation. However, I did not have this document at the time. But I wanted to give an additional answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand Mr. Demurenko but I'm not receiving any interpretation. There was no interpretation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would the court deputy have that looked into, or the technical staff. Are you receiving any now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to draw your attention to the fact, and I'm saying this for the third time, the attempt to show indirectly my alleged bias in favour of the Serbs is improper. The Prosecutor just said that Mr. Demurenko was waving with this drawing in front of the Serbian television cameras, and I need to tell you that I never gave a statement to the Serbian television. I gave a statement to Associated Press, the US agency representative. And now to try and to depict me as somebody who is a supporter of the Serbian side, that is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, I would like to ask you to comment on this drawing. What do these two lines represent, the trajectory of the shell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I object. The witness just said he did not have this document at that time. This is an exhibit that's been on the record for a while. It could have been shown to the witness in the real examination-in-chief. And we had similar exhibits before then exactly depicting this angle of descent. I didn't raise it in cross-examination. We could go on forever with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tapuskovic will not be allowed to go on forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we had ruled that Mr. Tapuskovic would be allowed to put questions on documents brought by this witness to support his line of argument. I will allow the question irrespective of the fact that this was already an exhibit. Mr. Tapuskovic, we have to move quickly. The 40 minutes are up and I will allow you to proceed until the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will conclude by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please give us your comment. How does it relate to your earlier assessment? And could you comment on the trajectories, the left line and the right line, and various information about the angles. Can you give us the explanation? What does the first trajectory line show, the one on the left?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, it's difficult to comment on this, not knowing the author himself and not knowing what he was trying to sell. But if we distance ourselves from this, then I can tell you that the left trajectory is showing an angle as determined by the expert. And this trajectory goes right by the building. So if you -- as you can understand, this angle could not have been any narrower. Otherwise, the mortar would have hit the roof of the building and exploded there. I think that this angle, 67 to 88 degrees, is the correct one. At least it resembles a correct one. And as for the other angle showing 87 degrees, it was done in a shaky hand, so to speak, and it seems to be an unconvincing argument of the expert drawing this drawing. What were his reasons for drawing this trajectory, I couldn't tell you. We would need to hear his own explanation. And I can't draw any other conclusions based on this drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let us try to speed up. Let me show you some additional photographs made by you on this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-4406, that's the first photograph. Could we see that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, what are you pointing at?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, even though you can't see my face, it is obvious that this is my arm and my hand. I am pointing to the site which, according to calculations, could have been a firing position, and based on the photograph you can see that it was impossible to place a mortar in such an area. A mortar cannot fire from this location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. A mortar without the distance device, and that's precisely the kind of mortar that was used, such a shell will explode at any contact, which means that such a shell could have hit a branch and exploded right there on the spot killing the crew manning the mortar. And I don't think that there were any suicide-bent soldiers firing from a mortar there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recall the distance from Sarajevo between this point and the Markale market? Was that the 3.400 or the 3.600 metres' distance or was it at another point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already answered a similar question. To tell you the truth, I don't remember which photograph pertains to which particular firing position. I simply didn't write that down and I don't want to mislead you now. But I know that this was one of the possible firing positions as we established looking on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Demurenko, could it be said that each of these photographs - and I will show you just a couple of more - each of those photographs depicts one such possible firing position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely how it was. Each photograph was made in one particular occasion which had been identified in advance with a margin of error of 5 metres. My team and I travelled to these locations and took these photographs precisely in order to show that it was impossible to fire from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that explicitly earlier. In the vicinity of this location where you took this photograph, were you able to observe the entire area? Were you able to see whether there were any traces showing that a 120-millimetre mortar was placed in that area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, as we were approaching this spot, we observed the entire area around it, and had I seen 10 to 20 metres away from this spot a possible firing position, then yes, this could have been something that could have prompted me to draw some other conclusions in my investigation. However, there were no such traces anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing about what we see on the drawing. When you were pointing that finger, on the location where you were standing, actually, were there any traces of a mortar there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just spoken about that. Of course not. It would have been strange to catch me out standing exactly where the mortar had stood and pointing my finger somewhere else. My purpose -- the purpose of my inquiry was not to deceive or to mislead; it was to establish the truth. Knowing, having calculated, that the potential firing point was in the woods, I was pointing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I tender this photograph as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D357, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you two more photographs, not to show them all, and then finish. DD00-44066.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think that's probably a wrong number. They have little letters at the end. It's probably not a 6 but maybe a D or G or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my mistake. DD00-4406b. Your Honours, my assistant is not sure that the previous photograph has been admitted, that it received a number. Oh, yes, it did. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, look at this photograph. What you just said in relation to the previous photograph, does it also apply here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is an even more heavily wooded area. The trees are thicker. All the -- and it's quite clear that in this overgrown spot a firing point was untenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this photograph as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D358, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now see DD00-4406c.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's the previous one, just showing all of me, not only my arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have a photograph showing a meadow under that number. I don't know whether this was marked correctly. DD -- it's sheet number 13 of that document. Sorry, the letter at the end is E, not C.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We see the entire meadow here. You probably were able to see even a larger territory. Did you look at the entire meadow? Did you see anything that would have indicated the placement of a mortar at one point?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That photograph illustrates what I said; namely, that not all firing points, not all potential firing points, were placed in forests and woods, and this is precisely one that proves that point. It was not my fabrication in which I placed all the potential firing points in woods. This one happened to be in meadows. This was a perfectly clear meadow without any traces of vehicles that could have carried the mortar. No traces of a crater left by the base placed. No traces of powder, no traces of packaging. We see cattle grazing, but absolutely no trace of mortar placements, of firing. So the firing didn't come from here. I think this is the remote position, and on that satellite picture we saw a meadow. So this is either the most remote position or the second most remote position from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this photograph, Your Honours, as a Defence exhibit, and since I have no time to open any new subjects, I will finish my examination here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, just on the points relate to the -- relating to the new documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, and that's quite a number, but I try to limit myself. If we could go back to the Defence Exhibit D357. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, it looks like these are fortifications on that picture; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we getting it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we'll get it very soon, D357.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While that's being done, Colonel, it looks like these wooded beams portray a military fortification, something like that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember seeing that, but the purpose of that structure was not quite clear to me. I asked the same question when I came to that area of armed conflict. There were two possible explanations. Local inhabitants sometimes, on steep slopes, make such fortifications against landslides. It's just that the photograph doesn't show the territory behind me. Similar agricultural structures were later modified by the armies to serve as anti-infantry fortifications and obstacles that could impede the movement of machinery and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're saying that that could be either a military fortification or more simply a structure for agricultural purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to say is that in mountains in the Balkans, these were often made to prevent landslides, and they are usually under steep slopes protecting important structures, such as roads that could be destroyed by landslides. Later on, when the war began, when battles began, such structures were taken over by armies and modified to serve as fortifications and as obstacles. So they served a dual purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. But you're unable to tell us exactly where on a map that location is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said three times already that I would be deceiving you if I gave you exact X and Y coordinates on the map. I didn't even try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, today you said you had a kind of a GPS with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But as you know, the GPS system is not the Russian system called GLONASS. We used other countries' systems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let's hear Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is beyond the scope of my examination, at least I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's a new location, a new photo shown, and I'd like to know where it is. It goes to the credibility of the witness. I'd like to know how he figures out, you know, the exact location. That's the purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The question is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, last time when you testified, Colonel, you said that, and I quote you from page 777, that "unfortunately, at the time we didn't have a GPS device but we were able to use the traditional old-fashioned instruments to determine the location." So what's true now? Did you have a GPS system or did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is what I said 30 minutes ago. The system of global positioning has multiple functions. One cannot trust only the GPS or the Russian GPS system GLONASS or the instruments we had back in the days of the Soviet army. There are several more systems that enable you to find your position within a range of 5 to 15 metres. I used a number of them to ensure that we were really in the right place as determined by previous calculation and positioning on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There are only four or five locations you visited. You're unable to tell us where this location is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. In fact, I visited hundreds of locations. It's just that I have photos of four or five of them, you understand? The principle by which he found those sites, we went to the lowest point between the sites and then we found 170 degrees and went up the mountains in that line. It's only a flat line on the map, but it's kilometres in length that we crossed on foot. We visited hundreds of those locations, and in my mind it's like a very, very long and very dense film that I cannot rewind and replay right now in accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. I'm sorry, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's an honour to be called Mr. Tapuskovic. No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic is privileged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just to repeat what you told us before the break. You said the technique for you to visit these, as you call them, hundreds of places was you would go to the lowest point between the sites and then we found 170 degrees and went up on the mountains on that line, in that line. That's the way you proceeded to visit these locations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, basically, although travelling meant that we had to go on foot. Some places were so rocky and so steep that we had to travel in APCs to the closest point and then on foot. But in principle we walked hundreds of metres on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you focused on that line, on that 170 degrees. That was the purpose of you, to visit places along that 170-degree line.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to claim that it was 170 and not 176, then I'm afraid I would mislead the honourable Trial Chamber. All I know is that based on the material that you have, we made theoretical calculations as to the line that had to be verified and that was related to the initial investigation by the Bosnian authorities and UNPROFOR. But to claim that it was precisely 170 and not some other figure is something that I cannot do because I do not wish to mislead anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you followed one line, either 170 or 176. That was your guiding principle.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, these -- what you told us a moment ago, that you turned to AP as an international media that might be like that, but the only TV network that carried you was Bosnian Serb TV. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not true. My statement was broadcast by 110 agencies throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet. To say what, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not mind this question being put to the witness, but it is completely outside the scope of my examination earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe the witness referred himself in an answer to AP, saying that, you know, he was neutral, but I can leave that. No need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If P922 could be retrieved, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the drawing you referred to a moment ago. On this drawing you can see that the locations you looked at, the distances on that imaginary 176- or 170-degree line, are as follows: Within the Bosnian Serb territory, it's 2.700, 3.200, 3.600, and then it goes on to 4.000 -- 5.400. Now, 3.200 is wrong. That's a mistake. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I cannot make any claims about the accuracy of these figures on this line because one has to look this in the light of the entire material. This is how we have to look at this. And I'm not prepared to discuss the figures right now. I can discuss the principle but the figures themselves will not assist us when it comes to any conclusions, because it's not that they are contradictory but there are some differences in drawings and sketches so it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But look, Colonel, the importance of that is you rely on specific figures and you go out and check possible or impossible sites of mortars. And if these figures are wrong, if you go to sites that are based on the wrong data, we are looking at wrong places. You look at places that are just not accurate. Today you told us you went to the degree 170. Last time you told us 176. Today we now get a drawing which says 3.200 as one of the distances and last time you told us, and that's on the record, it's a figure of 3.400. If you look at the wrong place, how can you come and say it was impossible for the Bosnian Serbs to fire shells?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me repeat again that you're trying to catch me out when it comes to figures. You said that I claimed on one occasion 170 and then on another occasion 176. I'm not trying to do anything to prove anything with the figures, because it's very easy to make a mistake. Now you're saying that 3.200 is not correct, that previously I said 3.400. Let me repeat once again to you. In order for me to be quite accurate, I would need to spend two to three days with the figures, make my calculations using the firing tables, in order to be quite sure about the firing point. I walked this entire possible line of fire myself, on foot. I checked all the possible locations and I came to the conclusion that what the people were saying about the Serbian aggression and Serbian firing was not true. I personally walked on foot the entire trajectory and I established that there was absolutely no location where a mortar could have been placed. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest to you that you did that on a certain line, disregarding many other calculations that were more reliable, more accurate, than you had. I'm not saying it was bad faith for your side. I'm saying that the basis for your calculations to find these spots was inaccurate, was unreliable, not after the fact already at that time.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that there were no other calculations whatsoever. You cannot show me any other true, accurate calculation because nobody did them, and they didn't do them because it wasn't suitable. As soon as the spokesperson said that it was the Serbs, everybody became quiet, they nodded their heads in consent, saying yes, those were the Serbs, and there was no other alternative. So you cannot show me any other calculation because it simply does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The French engineers, and we have seen the document this morning, came to 160 degrees. That's quite a distance from not only 170 degrees, even 170 -- 176 degrees, even from 170 degrees. That leads you to entire different areas as you can see on that satellite picture. Were you aware at that time that the French cell - and you showed French documents - came to the conclusion that the degree was 160 degrees and not 176 degrees as you thought it was? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Degree of what? Of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In a circle of 360 degrees, it's 160 degrees. If you look at the clock, it would point about to 4.00 or perhaps 5.00, whereas 176 degrees is more to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will reply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. Let us have a direct reply. Are you aware that the French came to that conclusion? Are you aware of that? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware that there were no other conclusions. The word "conclusion" means a final conclusion. An angle is not a conclusion. A trajectory is also not a conclusion. It is just one of the aspects used in investigation. I simply didn't see any such evidence because it doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Never mind the word "conclusion" that I used, and I see nothing wrong with it. Are you aware that they made a determination that it was 160 degrees, not 176 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of such an official document. Such official document did not exist, and I'm telling you as the second in charge within the military contingent. The French troops were under my command as well. Had they reached a different conclusion, they would have had to report to me about that; otherwise, they would have been guilty of insubordination. And I'm not aware of any such conclusions reached by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. That's the answer then, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, on the sketch drawn by you still on the screen, you used the figure six -- 2.850 mils, and that equals, I suggest to you, exactly those 160 degrees that the French arrived at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this can be seen in Exhibit P357 at page 6. 2.850 mils equals 160 degrees, the conclusion the French arrived at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting to him that in his drawing here depicting a line 2.850 mil, he was in fact representing, seeking to represent, what the French had determined?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The only figure of 2.850 I know of is the figure the French used in their engineers report, and we can look at the sketch together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us ask him, then. Where did this figure come from? Why do you have it there, 2.850 mil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to establish that, one would have to look at the entire material that was produced in investigation. I would have to look at all of them in order to have a full picture. I don't know where this figure came from. Probably not from my head. It was based on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe we can look at -- and that's going to be my final question. There might be just one sub-question. But if we look at Prosecution Exhibit 357, at page 6, we see a sketch by the French engineers. And as you know, Mr. President, Judge Harhoff, the witness referred to a French sketch before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are Yugoslav documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It should be P357, at page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While that's being done, a hundred -- just my last sub-question. A 120-millimetre mortar is a mobile weapon, is it not? It can be put into several pieces and carried. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it can be disassembled into two or three parts. The aim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I appreciate this but I know that -- but it has nothing to do with my examination, my redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sure that we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, does this relate to any of the new documentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It does. The photos, the witness said, looking at photos, that it was impossible to bring a mortar there. But again, for the sake of time, we have a mortar expert coming soon, I withdraw that question. If we could have the next page of that exhibit, please, page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at this image. This, I suggest to you, is a sketch from Markale, and it has at the end the notion of 2.850 millieme equals 160 degrees. Was that the source of information for you to use 2.850 milliemes as your guiding principle to go on the line of 176 or perhaps 170 degree, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one second. Can I, in one sentence, give an answer to the previous question? It's quite important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to draw your attention to the fact that 120-millimetre mortar can be disassembled into two parts. One is a base plate and the other one is the trunk. The trunk is over 200 kilogrammes and the base plate is over 300 kilogrammes. I doubt that anywhere in the world you can find a soldier who will take it upon himself to carry personally any part of this 120-millimetre mortar. Even though it can be disassembled, one needs either an animal, such as a donkey, a camel or a horse, or a vehicle to transport such an artillery piece. So this was an indirect attempt to claim that this mortar could be carried by hand. Yes, small mortars, 60-millimetre and 80-millimetre mortars, can be carried by a person. And you won't find any person in the world, even Mr. Universe would not be able to carry a 120-millimetre mortar. As for your second question, I have not seen this sketch before. I believe that it was produced subsequently either by -- or by somebody who had these facts and produced a sketch later. This may be a probable drawing. However, I did not see it at the time. I have a feeling that this was not done by a soldier but rather by a senior officer who attempted post factum to recreate the events. This is what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The same French you refer to as a fact of insubordination a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If he was below the position taken by me, then yes, it was a case of insubordination. There was a French colonel who attempted to produce his own version subsequently. If this was produced by him, then he will be judged by God himself. As far as I know, nothing else was made. This is something that we should have discussed in our staff and there were two or three aspects that needed to be discussed. I would have been happy to discuss them at the time; however, everybody shut their mouth and I was the only one running around trying to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, the only person publicly accused of, and you acknowledge that, of insubordination was you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, any questions arising from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: None. Judge Harhoff has some questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, I have two questions for you before we close your testimony. The first question relates to something you said during your first testimony; I think it was on the 5th of July. You said in a couple of sentences that in your view, Sarajevo was under siege, and the reason I'm returning to this fact is that you are a military person and I would like to have your assessment of what you actually meant when you said that the city of Sarajevo was under siege. Can you clarify that to us.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd be happy to. The city was practically 90 per cent encircled by the Bosnian Serb army troops. On the one hand, one can claim that they were encircled, that they were under siege, because all the roads were blocked and there was very little space for manoeuvre. On the other hand, there was a tunnel under Mount Igman, under the airport, which permitted the people to supply humanitarian aid as well as weapons and allowed them to move troops, allowed the Bosnian Muslims to move troops. So if one looks at the human suffering, then it was a case of a full siege, just like in Leningrad during Second World War. And if one looks at the possibility to have military movements, then one can say that yes, it was possible and one could move 500 to 600 troops overnight through the tunnel. So yes, it was a case of siege but with certain qualification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is more difficult because, at least for me, I'm a bit puzzled by the conclusions that the Chamber can draw from your exercise in the field after the Markale incident. And this is why I thought I should put the question to you in a different line; namely, to ask you what was really the purpose of your action? And I can see two interpretations and I would like to put them to you in order to indicate to me and to the Chamber whether it was one or the other or perhaps a third interpretation. My first interpretation is that you were unhappy about the facts that some UN spokesman, I think it was a British press officer associated to the UN, who stood out very quickly, a couple of hours perhaps, after the incident and declared publicly on behalf of the United Nations that the shelling had been done by the Serbs. And you felt that he was doing that without any proper basis and so therefore the purpose of your action was simply to say, No, at this point in time it is impossible to establish who fired the shot, and all I want to do is to say that at this point it is impossible to have any opinion about which of the two sides fired the mortar. And that was what you wanted to say and nothing more. That is one interpretation. The other interpretation is that you felt bad about the fact that the Serbs were being blamed for the shot and that therefore your primary purpose was to show that it couldn't have been the Serbs and that's why you went to the field, to establish that, according to the data that were available to you at the time, the Serbs could not have fired the mortar because at each one of the points from which this mortar could have been fired it was impossible to fire a mortar, either because it was too rocky or too hilly or because there was too much wood, or where eventually you found that it would have been possible, then at those places you found no traces of a launching. And it makes a difference to the Chamber which of the two interpretations you really had. Could you clarify this to us.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that most important question. I'll be frank and I'll say, I hope you agree with me that there are few people, especially in a rushed situation, in wartime, who could make a decision in a split second and then a week later, with all the things they have learned in the meantime, they didn't regret the decision or change their mind. I am not one of those few people, even if they exist. So it's probably the case of a third motivation that is a combination of the two you mentioned. I'll try to explain. By that time in August 1995, I was really sick and tired, totally fed up with this overwhelming deceit from all sides and the portraying of Serbs as culprits for everything, including those who were supposed to be international representatives, honest people, impartial, unbiased. Even they either kept their silence or even contributed to that general media frenzy. So by August I was really fed up with that. And the statement made by the spokesman was the last straw that broke the camel's back and prompted me to overstep my authority. On one hand, it was not the job of a rather highly placed officer to run around in fields and across hills. I was not a lowly soldier at that time; I was rather highly placed. But I wanted to check for myself, not simply entrust it to a lieutenant or a major. And I also wanted to expose the spokesman and his lie, as well as those who proceeded to comment and further disseminate his version, that it was the work of Serbs. And in the course of my work this essence, this purpose, became clearer and clearer until it became crystal clear. My goal was to show that the spokesman was lying, or at least jumped the gun when he had no grounds to say that, and the spokesman represented the entire organisation of the UN. This was heard throughout the world and I wanted to put a stop to that. That was one purpose. And another objective was that if the spokesman said this was done by Serbs, I wanted to show that there can be no certainty. There was no certainty at that time and an inquiry was called for. Since nobody showed any initiative, not even the superior UN BH command, nor anyone in our sector, the sector of Sarajevo, I took the initiative upon myself. That's it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. But it seems as if you're saying that it could, indeed, have been the Serbs who fired the shot and that your objection was really that at that time it was impossible to say so. But it could have been the Serbs or it could have been the Bosnians -- the Bosniak, the ABH, ABiH. Both options were possible and the only thing that you were saying was that at that time no one could be sure. Is that how we should interpret it -- interpret your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interpreted narrowly, yes. But in the broader sense, you remember earlier on we mentioned a subject but we didn't develop it. I am 100 per cent sure that it was an internal terrorist act. A mine was set up very cleverly, very slyly, in a way to imitate a mortar mine. And anybody could have placed that mine under the Markale market. It could have been any local inhabitant, including an ethnic Serb. It was done locally, I was sure of that. I cannot, of course, claim that it was not by an ethnic Serb. But I am sure that it was done locally, from the spot itself, not in the way that was later presented by the UN and all the media. Later on, nobody had the political will or the desire to conduct a real investigation and find the real perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, this is news, because my question is, then, wouldn't it have been more proper to try and establish that this was not at all a mortar? You seem to act as if it had been a mortar shell. You were showing in television the handbook of the trajectory and you went out into the field and so everything you did seemed to be based on the assumption that it was, indeed, a mortar shell. Now you're saying that your personal belief was that it wasn't a mortar shell at all but some bomb that had been placed there and just made to have impacts similar to a mortar shell. This is a very bold possibility, but my question is, then, why on earth didn't you try to establish that more directly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to emphasise, and I think I spoke about that back in July but nobody allowed me to develop that subject because it seemed to be a distraction from the main topic. Before talking about a terrorist act, I had first to prove that it was not a mortar explosion. But after receiving approval, I had first to prove that it was not a Serbian mortar attack and then to prove that it was not a Bosnian -- Bosniak mortar attack either, and then I could have proceeded. But nobody allowed me to go, to move on to the Bosniak segment of it because it was inconceivable that their own troops would attack their own people. So only after having dealt with that could I have gone on to the second part, the terrorist act. And by the way, it was the subject of a lot of writing, a lot of analysis. Many people throughout the world, even after theoretical investigations, said that it was precisely the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Had it been the case that allegations were being made that the attack was launched by the Bosnian Muslims, and in circumstances where you felt that to be untrue, as you did in this case, would you have carried out an investigation and carried out -- carried it out with the same determination?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. There's no doubt about that. I was prepared to continue my pursuit of the truth as soon as I gave that interview and it all became known to my superiors. But as I told you at the last session, I took two decisions simultaneously -- or, rather, two decisions were made simultaneously. The Bosnian army decided to kill me, that's first, and my own superior command decided to send me back to Russia at the same time for insubordination allegedly, within 24 hours. Luckily I am still alive and the command was persuaded not to send me back because that would have looked like proof of my being right, and they decided to wait, apparently. A month later the Russian Federation decided to open an office in Mons, in the NATO headquarters, and that's where they sent me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to say thank you for your confidence and giving me this opportunity to share my views with you. Thank you. All the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, the next witness? Let me see if I can assist. Who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness is the expert, Ivan Stamenov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ivan Stamenov. I understand that it may take a little while for him to get here, since he's seated upstairs. In the meantime, I note that the Defence has filed a motion for adjudicated facts. You're in receipt of this, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was filed just recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The Prosecution was going to meet after court and talk about a response. I think we'll certainly have a response within the next 48 hours. We will not be taking anything like the two weeks envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right. That's the point. It's very late in the proceedings, Mr. Tapuskovic, so we need to deal with it as quickly as possible. I might just -- Mr. Docherty, in relation to the matter that we were discussing about the witness, the expert witness, we are not saying, are we, that an expert can't support a conclusion that he has made by relying on a source which may be very long, indeed. Please keep the witness outside for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So an expert could say, My conclusion is X and it is supported by this, and he would cite 30 pages from another source to support that single conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We're not only not saying that, Your Honour, but it would be our submission that experts should proceed in that way; that someone who has a doctoral degree in history, for example, and gives an opinion on Balkan history should be thoroughly conversant with the literature and able to rely upon it and synthesize it and put it into an appropriate report. There's nothing wrong with relying on someone else's work or saying I agree with the interpretation of Professor so and so. What is wrong -- and also to reiterate the point I was making earlier. What is evidence of a lack of expertise is simply wholesale lifting word for word from the work of another without attribution. I think that that raises a question, as we put in our written submission that one has hit one of these little spots that every expert has got where their expertise simply does not -- does not extend. And I'll also take the liberty of noting that that was in our written submission. I think that's the central point of our written submission. And although the Defence responded to our written submission and made some points, they chose not to contest that particular assertion by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that is wrong? Is it the lack of attribution? Because suppose he had, in fact, attributed it to the ICJ source.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you still have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I would still have an objection but it would not be -- it would be somewhat less forceful. If I may elaborate. Perhaps an example is a good way of proceeding. In making the written submission, we have tried to stay away from, although it is not entirely successful, questions of right and wrong and honesty and dishonesty. The central thrust of our written submission and of my oral submission this morning is that what we have here is circumstantial evidence of a lack of expertise, notwithstanding academic credentials. It lends support to that claim of lack of expertise that Dr. Prsic did not attribute his source, and by way of example, in our area of expertise, we are all lawyers, we are all criminal lawyers, and yet I'm sure there are types of criminal cases that all of us perhaps have not handled in our careers, have not been trained on, do not know the particular laws concerning these cases. Before coming here I was a specialist in fraud cases. I did not do a lot of other types of cases. I have a lack of expertise in those other cases, notwithstanding an academic degree in law and some years of experience. And I think that when Dr. Prsic finds it necessary to borrow another's work, we are seeing evidence of something analogous; that although he has an academic degree in history, in this particular area, he has a lack of expertise and therefore finds it necessary to borrow. And I think it makes that conclusion stronger when we see the lack of attribution because there we see an attempt to, bluntly, to fake it, to carry on as though the expertise did exist, as though this was in fact his work. And that, I think, is evidence of consciousness on the part of the expert of a lack of expertise. Listening to that, I'm not sure it's entirely clear. But that is how I'm trying to factor the lack of attribution into the central point, which is circumstantial evidence of lack of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to say anything on that, Mr. Tapuskovic? I'm just asking you. This is the adversarial system that you refer to all the time. Do you have any comment to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honours. I requested from and instructed the witness to provide as little information as possible regarding history, to offer the sources, but knowing that in a case like this, the historical background is secondary and almost marginal, especially in our particular situation, I insisted on brevity. This entire report has 30 or 50 pages, with references to sources, and we believed that the only thing worth focusing on was the period after the 1940s. If I gave him a free hand, we would have received a report of a thousand pages, like the Donja report, and we know that Professor Donja began in a time when the Slavs first came to the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Let the witness be brought in. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make the point. The report of Donja is nowhere near a thousand pages, even less than -- I think it's about 35 pages and it has two or three sentences about the past. I really take offence in characterising Mr. Donja's report the way the Defence did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we don't want to carry this on any further. Mr. Tapuskovic, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant no offence to anyone. I just asked my historian to be as brief as possible regarding historical elements, because I believe they are marginal in this case. And that's what I'm emphasising again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: Ivan Stamenov.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: 7 March 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: I'm a professional officer, colonel by rank. I work at the Military Academy of the Army of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, you are an active-duty officer at this moment, a colonel of the army of the state that is recently renamed Serbia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: Yes. I'm an active-duty colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just please try not to begin your answer before the cursor on the screen in front of you has stopped. Now, as you said, you were a colonel in the army in Serbia. What exactly is your job?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: I am chief of department of the weapons and military equipment for the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of weaponry are you dealing with and lecturing on at the military academy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: The department of weaponry and military equipment of the ground forces has a syllabus that includes infantry weapons, armoured and mechanised units, artillery, the equipment of engineering units, and nuclear, biological and chemical weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of your field of expertise as you described it, including infantry weapons, how long have you been a lecturer and a professor at the military academy, and also as a professional officer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: Infantry weapons are my narrow specialisation and I've been dealing with that since 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Those infantry weapons, which include sniper rifles, are all part of your expertise.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. All the weapons that I mentioned so far, I have studied all this time and teaching my students about, and that includes sidearms, personal weapons, pistols, rifles, sniper rifles, weapons for close range, anti-armour combat, including -- and also mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the theoretical knowledge you impart to your students is something different from practical knowledge. Do you also give any practical courses, apart from theoretical lectures?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: Yes. The curriculum envisages that students get some practical training, including target practice. That is regularly scheduled. And I, as a teacher, a lecturer, attend that target practice and I show a particular piece of weaponry that is being used on that day to the trainees and I demonstrate how it is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamenov, you're quite familiar with the electronic equipment, so I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that you are speeding and you need to follow the cursor on the screen. Please do not begin your reply until you see that the cursor has stopped. I'd like to ask you something else. You spoke of a hobby that you have when telling us about your career and you said that you were also an athlete, a marksman athlete. It's a hobby that complements your profession. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of my hobbies. In addition to that I'm an innovator and a sportsman, marksman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before the break, can you tell me another thing, at the request of the Defence, you produced a report on a number of sniper incidents from the indictment against the accused Dragomir Milosevic from the 10th of August, 1994, until the end of May 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since that document is in e-court, Your Honours, could we see DD00-4689 and could that be admitted into evidence. I don't think we have any time to proceed with further questions, I mean once you rule on the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D360.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we'll take the break. We'll resume tomorrow, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
